items.followUp: Define stress and strain, and write the formula for Young’s modulus in terms of force, area, original length and extension.

rubric.why: Checks the defining property of Young’s modulus as a material response to deformation.
rubric.description: Identifies Young’s modulus as the ratio of stress to strain within the elastic limit.
rubric.how: Award for stating the ratio and its elastic-limit condition; accept equivalent wording.

rubric.description: Writes the formula for Young’s modulus, including an equivalent form using force and dimensions.
rubric.how: Award for Y = stress/strain or an equivalent formula such as Y = FL/(AΔL).

modelAnswer: Young’s modulus is the ratio of stress to strain in a material, provided it is within its elastic limit.

items.followUp: What does a sudden rise in atmospheric pressure usually indicate about the weather?

rubric.why: Checks recognition that a falling barometer reading indicates a region of low atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: States that a sudden fall means atmospheric pressure is becoming low.
rubric.how: Award for identifying low pressure or an equivalent statement.

rubric.why: Checks the weather implication of the falling pressure.
rubric.description: States that a storm or rainy/bad weather is likely approaching.
rubric.how: Award for any suitable prediction of approaching stormy or rainy weather.

modelAnswer: A sudden fall in atmospheric pressure indicates that a low-pressure region is approaching.
It usually means that a storm or rainy weather may be approaching.

items.followUp: State Pascal’s law and name two devices that work on its principle.

rubric.why: Checks the central statement of Pascal’s law.
rubric.description: States that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished throughout it and to the container walls.
rubric.how: Award for the equal, undiminished transmission of applied pressure in an enclosed fluid.

rubric.why: Checks knowledge of practical applications of Pascal’s law.
rubric.description: Names two valid applications, such as a hydraulic press, hydraulic brakes or a hydraulic lift.
rubric.how: Award for any two distinct valid applications.

modelAnswer: Pascal’s law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions throughout the fluid and to the walls of its container.
Two applications are hydraulic brakes and a hydraulic press.

items.followUp: Define elastic limit and explain what happens when a material is stretched beyond it.

rubric.description: Defines elasticity as the property by which a body regains its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed.
rubric.how: Award for explaining recovery of original shape/size after removal of the force.

rubric.why: Checks that the student distinguishes the limit from the property of elasticity.
rubric.description: Defines elastic limit as the maximum deformation or stress up to which the body recovers its original shape; beyond it, permanent deformation occurs.
rubric.how: Award for the maximum recoverable limit and its consequence when exceeded.

modelAnswer: Elasticity is the property of a body by which it regains its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed.
The elastic limit is the maximum limit up to which a body regains its original shape after the force is removed; beyond it, permanent deformation occurs.

items.followUp: A couple consists of two forces of 8 N whose lines of action are 0.25 m apart. Find its torque.

rubric.why: Checks the defining features of a couple.
rubric.description: Defines a couple as two equal, opposite and parallel forces acting along different lines.
rubric.how: Award for the equal-and-opposite parallel force pair, with separation implied or stated.

rubric.why: Checks the mathematical expression for the couple’s torque.
rubric.description: Writes total torque of a couple as force multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the forces’ lines of action.
rubric.how: Award for τ = Fd or an equivalent expression defining d as the perpendicular separation.

modelAnswer: A couple is a pair of equal, opposite and parallel forces acting along different lines.
Its total torque (moment) is τ = Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the forces.

items.followUp: State the first condition of equilibrium and write its mathematical expression.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of rotational equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that the net torque on a body in rotational equilibrium is zero, or that clockwise and anticlockwise torques are equal.

rubric.why: Checks the mathematical expression of the second condition.
rubric.description: Writes the expression for rotational equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award for Στ = 0 or an equivalent equality of clockwise and anticlockwise torques.

modelAnswer: The second condition of equilibrium states that the sum of the torques acting on a body about any point is zero.
Στ = 0, or total clockwise torque = total anticlockwise torque.

items.followUp: A wheel rotates with constant angular speed. Does it satisfy the second condition of equilibrium? Explain briefly.

rubric.why: Checks the conclusion about a fan rotating at constant speed.
rubric.description: Answers that the fan satisfies the second condition of equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award for a clear affirmative answer.

rubric.why: Checks the physical reason that the resultant torque is zero during uniform rotation.
rubric.description: Explains that uniform angular speed means zero angular acceleration and hence zero resultant torque; driving and resistive torques may balance.
rubric.how: Award for relating uniform rotation to zero net torque or stating that the torques balance.

modelAnswer: Yes. A ceiling fan rotating with uniform speed has zero angular acceleration.
Therefore, the resultant torque on it is zero, so it satisfies the second condition of equilibrium.

items.followUp: Describe how a thermal power station uses natural gas to generate electricity.

rubric.why: Checks the initial energy conversion when fossil fuel is burned.
rubric.description: States that burning fossil fuel converts its chemical energy into heat energy.
rubric.how: Award for the chemical-to-heat conversion or equivalent wording.

rubric.why: Checks the main steps by which the heat is used to generate electricity.
rubric.description: Explains that heat produces steam, which turns a turbine connected to a generator to produce electricity.
rubric.how: Award for the steam–turbine–generator sequence or an equivalent description.

modelAnswer: Burning fossil fuels converts their chemical energy into heat energy.
The heat boils water to produce steam; the steam turns a turbine connected to a generator, producing electricity.
